svg.text: Before: source dependencies follow control flow (Fig 5.1)
Control flows from HL1 to ML1 at runtime (HL1 simply calls F() in ML1; the interface exists only in source), but the source dependency from ML1 to the interface points
the opposite way. Any source dependency can be inverted by inserting an interface, so the architect has absolute control over dependency direction instead of it being
dictated by control flow (a caller had to #include, import or use the callee's module).
What you can do with it (Fig 5.3)
make the database and the UI depend on the business rules: they become plugins; the
business rules' source never mentions them; compile three components (jar, DLL,
Gem) with the same dependencies as the source; the rules do not depend on the UI or
change the UI or database and only that component is redeployed; independently
deployable modules can be developed independently by different teams. OO, for the
architect: absolute control of every source dependency, a plugin architecture with
high-level policy independent of low-level detail
